lessons.title: Forming a differential equation
lessons.summary: Translate proportional rates, gains and losses into a differential equation, and use observations to determine its constants.
lessons.objective: Define the quantities, form a signed rate equation, calibrate a proportionality constant and test its meaning.
lessons.before: Recall derivatives as instantaneous rates and the chain rule for related quantities.
lessons.ideas:
If \(q\) decreases at a rate proportional to itself, write \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=-kq\) with \(k>0\). Use one observed pair of amount and instantaneous rate to determine \(k\).

\(R\propto d^{-2}\) becomes \(R=\frac{k}{d^2}\). Solve for \(k\) by multiplying by \(d^2\).

The net rate equals gain rate minus loss rate. Solve “net rate = 0” to find a balance value, then use the sign to determine whether the quantity is rising or falling.
lessons.method:
1. Define the variables and sign
  2. Write the divisor
  3. Combine signed rates
  4. Use the signed difference
  5. Use the chain rule
mistakes: Do not use a negative proportionality constant as well as the explicit minus sign. That would model growth.
Only the quantity named in the proportionality phrase goes in the denominator. A greater positive distance gives a smaller rate.
A statement about the net rate does not say the inlet or outlet is zero. They can be equal and non-zero.

examples.title: Calibrate a proportional decrease
examples.question: The amount \(q\) of dye in a display cell is measured in milligrams. It decreases at a rate proportional to the amount present. When \(q=9\), its rate of change is \(-3\,\mathrm{mg\,min^{-1}}\). Write the model as \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=-kq\). Find \(k\) and the signed rate when \(q=12\).
examples.solution:
A decrease has a negative signed derivative. Use \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=-kq\) with \(k>0\).

The calibration gives \(3=9 k\), so \(k=\frac{1}{3}\) per minute.

At the new amount the derivative is \(-kq=-4\) milligrams per minute.

examples.title: Write an inverse rate model
examples.question: The output \(I\) of a device increases at a rate inversely proportional to the distance \(d\) from a fixed source. At \(d=3\) its rate of increase is \(2\). Find \(k\) in \(\frac{\mathrm dI}{\mathrm dt}=\frac{k}{d}\) and the rate when \(d=5\).
examples.solution:
Inversely proportional places the distance beneath the fraction bar.

Multiply the observed rate by \(d\) to obtain \(k=6\).

The predicted rate at the new distance is \(\frac{6}{5^{1}}\) or \(\frac{6}{5}\).

examples.title: Combine gain and loss rates
examples.question: An illuminated track gains \(17\) units of charge per minute and loses \(3\) times the current charge \(q\) each minute. Find the signed derivative at \(q=3\) and the charge for which the derivative is zero.
examples.solution:
The gain and loss are both rates. Subtract the loss to write \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=17 - 3 q\).

Substitute the observed charge to obtain \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=8\).

At balance, \(17=3 q\), so \(q=\frac{17}{3}\).

examples.title: Combine gain and loss rates
examples.question: An illuminated track gains \(21\) units of charge per minute and loses \(5\) times the current charge \(q\) each minute. Find the signed derivative at \(q=5\) and the charge for which the derivative is zero.
examples.solution:
The gain and loss are both rates. Subtract the loss to write \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=21 - 5 q\).

Substitute the observed charge to obtain \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=-4\).

At balance, \(21=5 q\), so \(q=\frac{21}{5}\).

lessons.title: General solutions by integration
lessons.summary: Recover a family of curves from its gradient. Choose an antiderivative, keep one arbitrary constant and check by differentiating.
lessons.objective: Integrate a rate depending on the independent variable and explain the role of the arbitrary constant.
lessons.before: Recall the integration rules for powers, linear exponents, reciprocals and trigonometric functions.
lessons.ideas:
Use \(\int x^n\,\mathrm dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C\) when \(n e-1\). Integrate a sum term by term.

For \(k e0\), an antiderivative of \(\mathrm e^{kx}\) is \(\frac1k\mathrm e^{kx}\). Check the coefficient by differentiating.

\(\int\frac{a}{bx+c}\,\mathrm dx=\frac ab\ln|bx+c|+C\) for \(b e0\) on an interval avoiding \(bx+c=0\).
lessons.method:
1. Integrate a power and a constant
  2. Undo the chain multiplier
  3. Integrate a linear reciprocal
  4. Integrate sine and cosine
  5. Differentiate back to the gradient
mistakes: A constant on the right-hand side integrates to a term in x. The arbitrary integration constant is a separate term.
Do not increase the exponent as with a power of x. The linear exponent remains the same.
A solution obtained by integrating through a reciprocal is defined separately on either side of its pole.

examples.title: Integrate a polynomial gradient
examples.question: The equation \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=3 x^{2} - 2\) has a general solution of the form \(y=ax^3+bx+C\). Find the two displayed coefficients.
examples.solution:
The right-hand side depends only on \(x\), so integrate with respect to \(x\).

Raise each power by one and divide its coefficient by the new power. The constant gradient integrates to a multiple of x.

Write \(y=x^{3} - 2 x+C\). Differentiation removes \(C\) and gives \(3 x^{2} - 2\).

examples.title: Reverse the chain factor of an exponential
examples.question: The equation \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=2 e^{3 x} - 2\) has a general solution of the form \(y=a\mathrm e^{3x}+bx+C\). Find the two displayed coefficients.
examples.solution:
The right-hand side depends only on \(x\), so integrate with respect to \(x\).

Differentiating the exponential brings out its inner coefficient. Divide by that coefficient when integrating.

Write \(y=- 2 x + \frac{2 e^{3 x}}{3}+C\). Differentiation removes \(C\) and gives \(2 e^{3 x} - 2\).

examples.title: Spot a logarithmic antiderivative
examples.question: The equation \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=2 + \frac{3}{2 x + 1}\) has a general solution of the form \(y=a\ln|2x+1|+bx+C\). Find the two displayed coefficients.
examples.solution:
The right-hand side depends only on \(x\), so integrate with respect to \(x\).

The numerator is constant and the denominator is linear. Divide by the derivative of the denominator when integrating the reciprocal.

Write \(y=\frac{3}{2}\ln|2x+1|+2x+C\). Differentiation removes \(C\) and gives \(2 + \frac{3}{2 x + 1}\).

examples.title: Spot a logarithmic antiderivative
examples.question: The equation \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=2 + \frac{7}{3 x + 1}\) has a general solution of the form \(y=a\ln|3x+1|+bx+C\). Find the two displayed coefficients.
examples.solution:
The right-hand side depends only on \(x\), so integrate with respect to \(x\).

The numerator is constant and the denominator is linear. Divide by the derivative of the denominator when integrating the reciprocal.

Write \(y=\frac{7}{3}\ln|3x+1|+2x+C\). Differentiation removes \(C\) and gives \(2 + \frac{7}{3 x + 1}\).

lessons.title: Separating variables
lessons.summary: Recognise separable equations, integrate each variable on its own side, and check restrictions introduced when dividing.
lessons.objective: Separate a product of factors, choose the integration method for each side and record any constant solutions that division excluded.
lessons.before: Recall integration of powers and reciprocals, logarithms and the partial-fraction decomposition of a rational function.
lessons.ideas:
For \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=f(x)g(y)\) on a branch where \(g(y) e0\), integrate \(\int\frac{1}{g(y)}\,\mathrm dy=\int f(x)\,\mathrm dx\).

\(\int\frac1y\,\mathrm dy=\ln|y|+C\). Drop the absolute values only when the sign is known and the resulting argument is positive.

For two distinct linear factors, choose one constant numerator for each denominator. Clear denominators to determine those constants before integrating.
lessons.method:
1. Separate powers
  2. Integrate reciprocals
  3. Split the rational side
  4. Choose each integration method
  5. Check zero factors separately
mistakes: Integrate each side with respect to its own variable. Multiplying the integrated equation by a constant also multiplies any integration constant, which can be renamed.
The logarithm may appear on both sides. Look for a chain multiplier on each side.
Do not integrate a product as a product of integrals. The equivalent sum is what can be integrated term by term.

examples.title: Separate a reciprocal power of y
examples.question: For \(x>0,\ y>0\), \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{2 x^{2}}{y}\). The general solution can be written as \(y^{2}=ax^{3}+C\). Find \(a\).
examples.solution:
Multiply by the power of \(y\) from the denominator to isolate \(y\) terms on the left.

Integrating gives \(\frac{y^{2}}{2}=\frac{2 x^{3}}{3}+C_1\).

Multiply by \(2\) and rename the arbitrary constant. The result is \(y^{2}=C + \frac{4 x^{3}}{3}\).

examples.title: Recognise logarithms on both sides
examples.question: For \(x>0,\ y>0\), \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{3 y}{2 x + 1}\). Write the integrated relation as \(\ln y=a\ln(2 x + 1)+C\). Find \(a\).
examples.solution:
Divide by \(y\), which is positive, so the left integrand is \(\frac{1}{y}\).

The right-hand side is a constant over a linear expression. Its antiderivative contains a factor \(\frac{1}{2}\).

Therefore \(\ln y=C + \frac{3 \log{\left(2 x + 1 \right)}}{2}\).

examples.title: Use partial fractions after separation
examples.question: A positive function satisfies \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\left(y + 4\right) \left(2 y + 4\right)\). Find \(a,b\) such that the integrated relation is \(a\ln(y + 2)+b\ln(y + 4)=2x+C\).
examples.solution:
Divide by the product of the positive linear factors.

The partial fractions of \(\frac{1}{\left(y + 2\right) \left(y + 4\right)}\) are \(- \frac{1}{2 \left(y + 4\right)} + \frac{1}{2 \left(y + 2\right)}\) when written with separate denominators.

Integrating gives \(\frac{\log{\left(y + 2 \right)}}{2} - \frac{\log{\left(y + 4 \right)}}{2}=C + 2 x\), so the two coefficients have opposite signs.

examples.title: Use partial fractions after separation
examples.question: A positive function satisfies \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\left(y + 7\right) \left(4 y + 16\right)\). Find \(a,b\) such that the integrated relation is \(a\ln(y + 4)+b\ln(y + 7)=4x+C\).
examples.solution:
Divide by the product of the positive linear factors.

The partial fractions of \(\frac{1}{\left(y + 4\right) \left(y + 7\right)}\) are \(- \frac{1}{3 \left(y + 7\right)} + \frac{1}{3 \left(y + 4\right)}\) when written with separate denominators.

Integrating gives \(\frac{\log{\left(y + 4 \right)}}{3} - \frac{\log{\left(y + 7 \right)}}{3}=C + 4 x\), so the two coefficients have opposite signs.

lessons.title: Initial conditions and particular solutions
lessons.summary: Use a given point to find the integration constant, choose a branch, and state where a particular solution is valid.
lessons.objective: Choose the particular curve through a given point and specify any necessary sign or interval restriction.
lessons.before: Recall the general family from separation, how to exponentiate both sides and how to solve inequalities in a radicand.
lessons.ideas:
First write the family with its free constant. Then use the condition to find the constant and rewrite the particular solution.

\(\ln|y|=F(x)+C\) gives \(y=A\mathrm e^{F(x)}\) on a non-zero branch, where the sign of \(A\) comes from the point.

Use the non-zero initial \(y\) or the sign of the shifted output, such as \(y+b\), to determine the sign in front of the square root.
lessons.method:
1. Find the constant from a point
  2. Restore the sign
  3. Choose the root using the initial sign
  4. Exclude an undefined derivative
  5. Follow the requested form
mistakes: The output value at a non-zero input is not generally the integration constant.
Using \(A=\mathrm e^C\) on a negative branch loses the minus sign. The point fixes both magnitude and sign.
A particular solution through a point has one branch. A final \(\pm\) retains a branch that fails the condition.

examples.title: Use a condition away from zero
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=4 x + 3\) with \(y=11\) at \(x=1\). Find the integration constant in \(y=C + 2 x^{2} + 3 x\) and the value at \(x=2\).
examples.solution:
Integrate first to obtain \(y=C + 2 x^{2} + 3 x\).

Insert both coordinates of the given condition. The resulting constant is \(C=6\).

Use that value to obtain \(y=2 x^{2} + 3 x + 6\), then find \(y=20\) at the requested input.

examples.title: Choose the correct sign after exponentiating
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=2 y\) with \(y=6\) at \(x=0\). Give the coefficient \(A\) in \(y=A\mathrm e^{2x}\) and state its sign.
examples.solution:
On a branch with \(y e0\), separation gives \(\ln|y|=C + 2 x\).

Exponentiating gives \(|y|=\mathrm e^C\mathrm e^{2x}\). Restore the sign as part of the coefficient \(A\).

At \(x=0\) the exponential is one, so \(A=6\) and \(y=6 e^{2 x}\).

examples.title: Select the square-root branch
examples.question: For \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{x}{y}\), use \(y=5\) at \(x=1\). Find \(C\) in \(y^2=C + x^{2}\), then give the exact value at \(x=2\).
examples.solution:
Multiply by \(y\) and integrate. After multiplying through by two, \(y^2=C + x^{2}\).

The initial point gives \(C=24\).

The positive square root agrees with the given point. Use \(y=\sqrt{x^{2} + 24}\) to obtain \(y=2 \sqrt{7}\).

examples.title: Select the square-root branch
examples.question: For \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{3 x}{y}\), use \(y=7\) at \(x=3\). Find \(C\) in \(y^2=C + 3 x^{2}\), then give the exact value at \(x=4\).
examples.solution:
Multiply by \(y\) and integrate. After multiplying through by two, \(y^2=C + 3 x^{2}\).

The initial point gives \(C=22\).

The positive square root agrees with the given point. Use \(y=\sqrt{3 x^{2} + 22}\) to obtain \(y=\sqrt{70}\).

lessons.title: Interpreting solutions in context
lessons.summary: Use a solved model to find times and rates, distinguish limits from thresholds, and state where a model remains meaningful.
lessons.objective: Read a limit, solve a threshold equation, find a signed rate and explain any endpoint or extrapolation restriction in context.
lessons.before: Recall initial conditions, the sign of exponential corrections and solving an exponential equation with logarithms.
lessons.ideas:
For \(Q=L+A\mathrm e^{-kt}\) with \(k>0\), the limit is \(L\). If \(A e0\) the model never equals \(L\) at a finite time.

Solve for the exponential before taking logs. Check the sign and units of the resulting time.

Solve for the boundary of the physical interval. Check whether the question includes that boundary and whether the differential equation itself holds there.
lessons.method:
1. Separate a level and a correction
  2. Isolate the decaying quantity
  3. Decide whether to include the endpoint
  4. Use the original relation or differentiate
  5. Compare with the stated constraints
mistakes: The limiting level is not the initial value. The initial value is \(L+A\).
Taking a log of the whole sum does not split it into logs of the terms. Subtract the constant level first.
Do not extend a model for a thickness, mass or volume to negative values without justification.

examples.title: Identify the limiting level and the direction
examples.question: A temperature model is \(T=12 + 24 e^{- \frac{2 t}{5}}\) for \(t\ge0\). Find the limiting temperature and decide whether the temperature approaches it from above or below.
examples.solution:
The exponential has a negative exponent coefficient, so it tends to zero as time increases.

The constant term remains, giving a limiting temperature of \(12\) degrees Celsius.

The correction term is positive at every finite time, so the temperature approaches from above.

examples.title: Calculate a threshold time exactly
examples.question: A sampling signal is \(S=15 + 16 e^{- \frac{t}{2}}\) for \(t\ge0\). It reaches \(23\) at \(t=a\ln b\) with \(b>1\). Give \(a,b\), using the integer \(b\) obtained by isolating the exponential and taking its reciprocal.
examples.solution:
Subtract the constant level and divide by the initial offset. This gives \(e^{- \frac{t}{2}}=\frac{1}{2}\).

Take logarithms. Equivalently, invert first to make the exponent positive and the argument an integer.

The time is \(t=2 \log{\left(2 \right)}\). It is positive because the signal falls towards its limit.

examples.title: Stop a model when its quantity reaches zero
examples.question: An ice layer melts according to \(h=3 - t\), where \(h\) is its thickness in millimetres and \(t\) is time in minutes. Include the instant it disappears. Give the valid time interval from the start and the thickness after one minute.
examples.solution:
The model starts at \(t=0\) with positive thickness.

Solve \(h=0\) to find \(t=3\). The interval of validity is \(0\le t\le 3\).

At one minute, the thickness is \(2\) millimetres.

examples.title: Stop a model when its quantity reaches zero
examples.question: An ice layer melts according to \(h=10 - 2 t\), where \(h\) is its thickness in millimetres and \(t\) is time in minutes. Include the instant it disappears. Give the valid time interval from the start and the thickness after one minute.
examples.solution:
The model starts at \(t=0\) with positive thickness.

Solve \(h=0\) to find \(t=5\). The interval of validity is \(0\le t\le 5\).

At one minute, the thickness is \(8\) millimetres.

questions.title: Calibrate a proportional decrease
questions.prompt_html: The amount \(q\) of dye in a display cell is measured in milligrams. It decreases at a rate proportional to the amount present. When \(q=21\), its rate of change is \(-7\,\mathrm{mg\,min^{-1}}\). Write the model as \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=-kq\). Find \(k\) and the signed rate when \(q=27\).
questions.solution_html:
A decrease has a negative signed derivative. Use \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=-kq\) with \(k>0\).

The calibration gives \(7=21 k\), so \(k=\frac{1}{3}\) per minute.

At the new amount the derivative is \(-kq=-9\) milligrams per minute.
questions.hint_html: Use the sign of the rate before finding the proportionality constant.

questions.title: Calibrate a proportional decrease
questions.prompt_html: The amount \(q\) of dye in a display cell is measured in milligrams. It decreases at a rate proportional to the amount present. When \(q=25\), its rate of change is \(-5\,\mathrm{mg\,min^{-1}}\). Write the model as \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=-kq\). Find \(k\) and the signed rate when \(q=32\).
questions.solution_html:
A decrease has a negative signed derivative. Use \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=-kq\) with \(k>0\).

The calibration gives \(5=25 k\), so \(k=\frac{1}{5}\) per minute.

At the new amount the derivative is \(-kq=- \frac{32}{5}\) milligrams per minute.
questions.hint_html: Use the sign of the rate before finding the proportionality constant.

questions.title: Write an inverse rate model
questions.prompt_html: The output \(I\) of a device increases at a rate inversely proportional to the square of the distance \(d\) from a fixed source. At \(d=5\) its rate of increase is \(5\). Find \(k\) in \(\frac{\mathrm dI}{\mathrm dt}=\frac{k}{d^2}\) and the rate when \(d=7\).
questions.solution_html:
Inversely proportional places the square of the distance beneath the fraction bar.

Multiply the observed rate by \(d^2\) to obtain \(k=125\).

The predicted rate at the new distance is \(\frac{125}{7^{2}}\) or \(\frac{125}{49}\).
questions.hint_html: Check that increasing the distance decreases the rate.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the correct rate at the new distance.

questions.title: Write an inverse rate model
questions.prompt_html: The output \(I\) of a device increases at a rate inversely proportional to the distance \(d\) from a fixed source. At \(d=6\) its rate of increase is \(6\). Find \(k\) in \(\frac{\mathrm dI}{\mathrm dt}=\frac{k}{d}\) and the rate when \(d=8\).

Inversely proportional places the distance beneath the fraction bar.

The predicted rate at the new distance is \(\frac{36}{8^{1}}\) or \(\frac{9}{2}\).

questions.title: Combine gain and loss rates
questions.prompt_html: An illuminated track gains \(23\) units of charge per minute and loses \(6\) times the current charge \(q\) each minute. Find the signed derivative at \(q=6\) and the charge for which the derivative is zero.
questions.solution_html:
The gain and loss are both rates. Subtract the loss to write \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=23 - 6 q\).

Substitute the observed charge to obtain \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=-13\).

At balance, \(23=6 q\), so \(q=\frac{23}{6}\).
questions.hint_html: Write rate in minus rate out, then set the derivative to zero for balance.

questions.title: Combine gain and loss rates
questions.prompt_html: An illuminated track gains \(25\) units of charge per minute and loses \(7\) times the current charge \(q\) each minute. Find the signed derivative at \(q=7\) and the charge for which the derivative is zero.
questions.solution_html:
The gain and loss are both rates. Subtract the loss to write \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=25 - 7 q\).

Substitute the observed charge to obtain \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=-24\).

At balance, \(25=7 q\), so \(q=\frac{25}{7}\).
questions.hint_html: Write rate in minus rate out, then set the derivative to zero for balance.

questions.title: Use the signed difference from a target
questions.prompt_html: A study pod adjusts to a target temperature of \(16^\circ\mathrm C\). The model is \(\frac{\mathrm dT}{\mathrm dt}=-k(T-16)\). At \(T=23\) the signed rate is \(-5\). Find \(k\) and the signed rate at \(T=10\).
questions.solution_html:
Use the difference from the target. At the observed temperature this difference is \(7\).

The falling rate gives \(k=\frac{5}{7}\).

Below the target, the bracket is negative. The model gives \(\frac{\mathrm dT}{\mathrm dt}=\frac{30}{7}\), so the temperature rises.
questions.hint_html: Test the sign by asking in which direction the temperature moves towards the target.

questions.title: Use the signed difference from a target
questions.prompt_html: A study pod adjusts to a target temperature of \(18^\circ\mathrm C\). The model is \(\frac{\mathrm dT}{\mathrm dt}=-k(T-18)\). At \(T=26\) the signed rate is \(-6\). Find \(k\) and the signed rate at \(T=11\).
questions.solution_html:
Use the difference from the target. At the observed temperature this difference is \(8\).

The falling rate gives \(k=\frac{3}{4}\).

Below the target, the bracket is negative. The model gives \(\frac{\mathrm dT}{\mathrm dt}=\frac{21}{4}\), so the temperature rises.
questions.hint_html: Test the sign by asking in which direction the temperature moves towards the target.

questions.title: Air filtration in a recording booth
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(q\) be the amount of airborne dust in milligrams in a booth. Dust enters at \(22\) milligrams per minute. The rate of removal is directly proportional to the amount present.

  1. Write a differential equation for \(q\) with a positive constant \(k\). [1]
  2. When \(q=8\), the amount is decreasing by \(2\) milligrams per minute. Find \(k\) and state its units. [3]
  3. Find the dust amount at which the net rate is zero and decide if the amount is rising or falling at \(q=5\). [3]
questions.solution_html:
1. Take the entry rate as positive. Remove \(kq\) from it to obtain \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=22-kq\).

  2. Use \(-2=22-8k\) to obtain \(k=3\).

    Since \(kq\) has units milligrams per minute, \(k\) has units per minute.

  3. \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=0\) gives \(q=\frac{22}{3}\). At \(q=5\) the derivative is \(22-15=7\), which is positive.
questions.hint_html: Write the derivative as gain minus loss. Leave the loss coefficient unknown until using the observation.

marking_criteria.description_html: Write the positive gain and negative proportional loss in a single differential equation.
Use the signed rate at the given amount.
Use a signed rate to conclude the amount is rising.

questions.title: A shrinking circular light patch
questions.prompt_html:
A circular illuminated patch has radius \(r\) centimetres and area \(A\) square centimetres at time \(t\) minutes. The area decreases at a rate proportional to \(r^2\). When \(r=2\), the area is decreasing by \(6\pi\) square centimetres per minute.

  1. Write the area-rate equation with a positive constant \(k\) and find \(k\). [3]
  2. Form an equation for \(\frac{\mathrm dr}{\mathrm dt}\) that is valid for \(r>0\). [2]
  3. Find the signed radius rate when \(r=5\) and explain the restriction \(r>0\) in part (b). [2]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(\frac{\mathrm dA}{\mathrm dt}=-kr^2,\quad k=\frac{3\pi}{2}\)
  2. \(\frac{\mathrm dr}{\mathrm dt}=-\frac{3r}{4}\)
  3. \(-\frac{15}{4}\,\mathrm{cm\,min^{-1}}\). The division uses a non-zero radius.
questions.solution_html:
1. Use \(\frac{\mathrm dA}{\mathrm dt}=-kr^2\). Then \(-6\pi=-4k\) gives \(k=\frac{3\pi}{2}\).

  2. \(\frac{\mathrm dA}{\mathrm dt}=2\pi r\frac{\mathrm dr}{\mathrm dt}\) by the chain rule.

    Equate to \(-\frac{3\pi}{2}r^2\) and divide by \(2\pi r\) to get \(\frac{\mathrm dr}{\mathrm dt}=-\frac{3r}{4}\).

  3. At \(r=5\) the derivative is \(-\frac{15}{4}\) centimetres per minute.

    The chain-rule rearrangement divides by \(r\). The illuminated region also has positive radius while it exists.
questions.hint_html: Use \(A=\pi r^2\) to relate the area rate to the radius rate.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the chain rule for the area.
Explain the restriction using the division or the physical model.

questions.title: A balance for a coating bath
questions.prompt_html:
The quantity \(q>0\) in a coating bath increases due to an inlet of five units per minute. Extraction removes units at a rate inversely proportional to \(q\). At \(q=4\) the signed net rate is \(-3\).

  1. Form the net-rate equation and find its constant. [3]
  2. Find all positive quantities for which the net rate is non-negative. [2]
  3. Calculate the inlet rate that would make \(q=8\) a constant solution, with the extraction coefficient unchanged. [2]
questions.solution_html:
1. Write \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=5-\frac{k}{q}\). The observation gives \(-3=5-\frac{k}{4}\) so \(k=32\).

  2. Since \(q>0\), multiply \(5-\frac{32}{q}\ge0\) by \(q\) without reversing the inequality.

    Then \(5q\ge32\) gives \(q\ge\frac{32}{5}\).

  3. At \(q=8\) the loss is \(\frac{32}{8}=4\). A constant solution requires the inlet rate to equal this rate.
questions.hint_html: The extraction term is a positive constant divided by the current quantity.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the correct inverse term and sign.
Set up and rearrange the inequality with q positive.
Give the complete range with equality included.

questions.title: A gradient that needs integration by parts
questions.prompt_html:
A family of curves satisfies \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=(2x-1)\mathrm e^x\).

  1. Find the general solution. [2]
  2. Find \(y(1)-y(0)\) exactly, and explain why it is the same for every curve in the family. [2]
  3. Give the input at which each curve is stationary and classify the stationary point. [3]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(y=(2x-3)\mathrm e^x+C\)
  2. \(3-\mathrm e\). The constant cancels.
  3. \(x=\frac12\) gives a local minimum.
questions.solution_html:
1. Use integration by parts with \(u=2x-1\) and \(\mathrm dv=\mathrm e^x\,\mathrm dx\).

    It gives \(y=(2x-1)\mathrm e^x-2\mathrm e^x+C=(2x-3)\mathrm e^x+C\).

  2. The values are \(y(1)=-\mathrm e+C\) and \(y(0)=-3+C\). Their difference is \(3-\mathrm e\).

  3. The exponential is positive, so zero gradient means \(2x-1=0\).

    The derivative changes from negative to positive at \(x=\frac12\). This is a minimum.
questions.hint_html: Integrate the polynomial factor by decreasing its degree.

questions.title: Find the primitive by substitution
questions.prompt_html:
A curve has gradient \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{9x}{\sqrt{4+3x^2}}\).

  1. Using \(u=4+3x^2\), find the general solution. [3]
  2. Find the change in \(y\) between \(x=0\) and \(x=2\). [2]
  3. Give the value of \(C\) for the curve through \((2,1)\) and find its y-intercept. [2]
questions.solution_html:
1. \(\mathrm du=6x\,\mathrm dx\), so \(\int\frac{9x}{\sqrt{4+3x^2}}\,\mathrm dx=\frac32\int u^{-\frac12}\,\mathrm du\).

    The antiderivative is \(3\sqrt u+C\), giving \(y=3\sqrt{4+3x^2}+C\).

  2. At the endpoints the square roots are \(2\) and \(4\). The change is \(3(4-2)=6\).

  3. At \(x=2\) the solution is \(y=12+C\), so \(C=-11\).

    At \(x=0\) the solution is \(y=6-11=-5\).
questions.hint_html: The derivative of the expression under the square root is proportional to the numerator.

questions.title: Use a trigonometric identity before integrating
questions.prompt_html:
A family of curves satisfies \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=1+2\cos^2(2x)\).

  1. Use a double-angle identity to find the general solution. [3]
  2. Find the exact change in \(y\) from \(x=0\) to \(x=\frac{\pi}{8}\). [2]
  3. Find the minimum possible gradient and determine the first strictly positive input at which it occurs. [3]
questions.solution_html:
1. Use \(2\cos^2(2x)=1+\cos(4x)\). The derivative is then \(2+\cos(4x)\).

    Integrate to obtain \(y=2x+\frac14\sin(4x)+C\).

  2. The sine terms at the ends are zero and one, respectively. The change is \(\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac14=\frac{\pi+1}{4}\).

  3. The form \(2+\cos(4x)\) has minimum \(2-1=1\).

    The first positive input with \(\cos(4x)=-1\) satisfies \(4x=\pi\), so \(x=\frac{\pi}{4}\).
questions.hint_html: Rewrite the squared cosine with the double-angle identity.

marking_criteria.description_html: Integrate the cosine with its chain factor.
Use the first positive minimum of the cosine.

questions.title: Separate a reciprocal power of y
questions.prompt_html: For \(x>0,\ y>0\), \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{5 x^{4}}{y^{4}}\). The general solution can be written as \(y^{5}=ax^{5}+C\). Find \(a\).
questions.solution_html:

Multiply by \(5\) and rename the arbitrary constant. The result is \(y^{5}=C + 5 x^{5}\).

questions.title: Recognise logarithms on both sides
questions.prompt_html: For \(x>0,\ y>0\), \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{4 y}{5 x + 4}\). Write the integrated relation as \(\ln y=a\ln(5 x + 4)+C\). Find \(a\).
questions.solution_html:
Divide by \(y\), which is positive, so the left integrand is \(\frac{1}{y}\).

The right-hand side is a constant over a linear expression. Its antiderivative contains a factor \(\frac{1}{5}\).

Therefore \(\ln y=C + \frac{4 \log{\left(5 x + 4 \right)}}{5}\).

questions.title: Use partial fractions after separation
questions.prompt_html: A positive function satisfies \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\left(y + 9\right) \left(5 y + 25\right)\). Find \(a,b\) such that the integrated relation is \(a\ln(y + 5)+b\ln(y + 9)=5x+C\).
questions.solution_html:
Divide by the product of the positive linear factors.

The partial fractions of \(\frac{1}{\left(y + 5\right) \left(y + 9\right)}\) are \(- \frac{1}{4 \left(y + 9\right)} + \frac{1}{4 \left(y + 5\right)}\) when written with separate denominators.

questions.title: Separate two linear factors
questions.prompt_html:
Consider \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=(x^2+1)(y+1)(y+4)\) with \(y>0\).

  1. Separate the variables and express the y-side integrand in partial fractions. [3]
  2. Find a general implicit solution with a single logarithm. [3]
  3. For the unrestricted original equation, find the constant solutions. [2]
questions.solution_html:
1. Divide by \((y+1)(y+4)\) and write the x-side as \((x^2+1)\,\mathrm dx\).

    Clearing denominators and using \(y=-1,-4\) gives coefficients \(\frac13,-\frac13\).

  2. Integrate the two partial fractions. The logarithms have positive arguments as \(y>0\).

    Multiply both sides by three, combine the logs and rename the constant.

  3. A constant function has zero derivative. The factor \(x^2+1\) cannot be zero for real \(x\), and the two real roots of \((y+1)(y+4)\) each give a constant solution.

questions.title: A substitution after separation
questions.prompt_html:
The equation is \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=6x\sqrt{1+x^2}(y-2)\) on a branch with \(y>2\).

  1. Show the separated equation and integrate both sides. [3]
  2. Give the explicit general solution on this branch and state the restriction on its multiplicative constant. [2]
  3. For this branch, state the value of \(x\) at which the gradient is zero and classify the stationary point. [2]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(\ln(y-2)=2(1+x^2)^{\frac32}+C\)
  2. \(y=2+A\mathrm e^{2(1+x^2)^{\frac32}},\ A>0\)
  3. \(x=0\) is a local minimum.
questions.solution_html:
1. \(\int\frac{1}{y-2}\,\mathrm dy=\int6x\sqrt{1+x^2}\,\mathrm dx\).

    With \(u=1+x^2,\ \mathrm du=2x\,\mathrm dx\), the right side is \(3\int u^{\frac12}\,\mathrm du=2u^{\frac32}+C\).

  2. Exponentiate to obtain \(y-2=\mathrm e^C\mathrm e^{2(1+x^2)^{\frac32}}\).

    Define \(A=\mathrm e^C>0\) and add two.

  3. Since \(y-2>0\) and \(\sqrt{1+x^2}>0\), the derivative has the sign of \(x\).

    It vanishes only at zero and changes from negative to positive there.
questions.hint_html: Use a logarithm on the y-side and set \(u=1+x^2\) on the x-side.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the indicated substitution with the correct multiplier.
Give the explicit solution and the positive constant restriction.
Identify the only zero of the derivative.
Use the sign change to classify the point.

questions.title: An inverse-tangent integral
questions.prompt_html:
Solve \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{6y}{x^2+9}\) over real \(x\).

  1. For \(y e0\), integrate the separated equation. [3]
  2. Give an explicit family incorporating every sign and the constant zero solution. [3]
  3. Find \(\frac{y(3)}{y(0)}\) for every non-zero branch. [2]
questions.solution_html:
1. Separate to obtain \(\int\frac1y\,\mathrm dy=\int\frac6{x^2+9}\,\mathrm dx\).

    The derivative of \(\tan^{-1}\left(\frac x3\right)\) is \(\frac3{x^2+9}\), giving the displayed result.

  2. Exponentiating gives \(|y|=\mathrm e^C\exp\left(2\tan^{-1}\left(\frac x3\right)\right)\).

    Use a signed constant \(A\). The value \(A=0\) is verified by direct substitution in the original equation.

  3. The coefficient cancels. At zero the inverse tangent is zero, and at three it is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\).

    The ratio is \(\mathrm e^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\).
questions.hint_html: On any non-zero branch, division by y leaves the standard inverse-tangent integral.

questions.title: Calculate a threshold time exactly
questions.prompt_html: A sampling signal is \(S=24 + 28 e^{- \frac{4 t}{5}}\) for \(t\ge0\). It reaches \(\frac{148}{5}\) at \(t=a\ln b\) with \(b>1\). Give \(a,b\), using the integer \(b\) obtained by isolating the exponential and taking its reciprocal.
questions.solution_html:
Subtract the constant level and divide by the initial offset. This gives \(e^{- \frac{4 t}{5}}=\frac{1}{5}\).

questions.title: A material sample approaches its target temperature
questions.prompt_html:
A sample has temperature \(T\) degrees Celsius at time \(t\) minutes. Its temperature satisfies \(\frac{\mathrm dT}{\mathrm dt}=-k(T-10)\) with \(k>0\). The temperatures at zero and two minutes are \(30\) and \(20\) degrees Celsius.

  1. Use the observations to determine the model for \(T\). [4]
  2. Find the time at which the sample reaches \(12.5\) degrees Celsius. [2]
  3. State the limiting temperature and explain whether it is attained at a finite time. [2]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(T=10+20\mathrm e^{-kt},\ k=\frac{\ln2}{2}\)
  2. \(6\) minutes.
  3. \(10\) degrees Celsius, approached from above and never attained at a finite time.
questions.solution_html:
1. Separate and integrate to get \(\ln(T-10)=-kt+C\) on the warm branch.

    At \(t=0\) the difference is \(20\), so \(T=10+20\mathrm e^{-kt}\).

    At two minutes the difference is \(10\), giving \(\mathrm e^{-2k}=\frac12\) and \(k=\frac{\ln2}{2}\).

  2. The new deviation is \(2.5\), or one eighth of the starting deviation. The difference halves every two minutes.

    Three halvings take six minutes.

  3. The exponential decreases to zero as \(t\to\infty\). At every finite time it is positive, so the sample remains above \(10\) degrees.
questions.hint_html: Use the temperature difference above ten to calibrate the decay.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the new deviation and the calibrated model.
Distinguish the limit from a finite-time value.

questions.title: Find the stopping time of a wear model
questions.prompt_html:
The thickness \(h\) of a protective coating, in millimetres, decreases according to \(\frac{\mathrm dh}{\mathrm dt}=-\frac1h\), with \(h=8\) at \(t=0\). Here \(t\) is measured in hours.

  1. Find the thickness as a function of \(t\) while it is positive. [3]
  2. Find when the thickness reaches four millimetres and give the signed rate then. [3]
  3. Give the time at which the model predicts disappearance and explain why the differential equation is used only before that instant. [2]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(h=\sqrt{64-2t}\)
  2. \(t=24\,\mathrm{h},\quad\frac{\mathrm dh}{\mathrm dt}=-\frac14\,\mathrm{mm\,h^{-1}}\)
  3. \(32\) hours, with the differential equation valid for \(0\le t<32\).
questions.solution_html:
1. Multiply by \(h\) and integrate to get \(\frac12h^2=-t+C\).

    The initial condition gives \(h^2=64-2t\). Use the positive square root.

  2. Set \(16=64-2t\) to get \(t=24\).

    Put \(h=4\) into the original rate equation, giving \(-\frac14\) millimetres per hour.

  3. At \(t=32\) the square root is zero. This is the limiting endpoint.

    The original right-hand side is undefined at zero thickness. Continuing also fails to give real positive thickness.
questions.hint_html: Select the positive square root, then check the original denominator at the endpoint.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the squared thickness to find the time.
Explain the restriction from either the denominator or the model domain.

questions.title: A fixed capacity limits the uptake
questions.prompt_html:
A sensor reports a quantity \(q\) that increases according to \(\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=k\left(1-\frac q{30}\right)\). Here \(t\) is in minutes, \(k>0\), \(q=6\) at zero and \(q=18\) at three minutes.

  1. By considering the gap \(u=30-q\), find the particular solution in terms of \(t\). [4]
  2. Find when \(q=27\). [2]
  3. Explain what happens to the growth rate in the long run and whether \(q=30\) occurs at any finite time. [2]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(q=30-24\exp\left(-\frac{\ln2}{3}t\right),\quad k=10\ln2\)
  2. \(9\) minutes.
  3. The rate tends to zero. The value \(30\) is approached and never attained at a finite time.
questions.solution_html:
1. The gap obeys \(\frac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm dt}=-\frac k{30}u\), so \(u=A\mathrm e^{-\frac k{30}t}\).

    Initially \(u=24\), and at three minutes \(u=12\). Hence \(\mathrm e^{-\frac k{10}}=\frac12\) and \(k=10\ln2\).

    Subtract the gap from thirty to obtain the solution.

  2. The gap is now three, an eighth of its initial value. The calibrated model halves the gap every three minutes, so the time is nine minutes.

  3. The remaining gap tends to zero and stays positive at each finite time.

    Since the rate is proportional to that gap, the growth rate tends to zero.
questions.hint_html: When a quantity is below its limit, track the remaining gap.

marking_criteria.description_html: Form the correct equation for the gap.
Find the gap solution using its initial value.
Use the other observation to determine the rate.
Apply the exponential model to the gap of three.
Justify why the capacity is not attained at finite time.
